Title:

Lifespan is mechanistically conserved across metazoans (11336665 \- Kenyon insulin review; 18340043 \- delete worm aging genes in yeast and find that they more often than not impact yeast aging; 17411345 \- Ruvkun finds essential worm genes that also extend lifespan and show they are conserved to humans; 28007498 \- oldish DR conservation review), varies among individuals of the same species and segregates heritable variation (27485207 \- my DSPR RIL mapping; 40326784 \- DO mouse mapping; 42020758 \- Rob williams 4-way mouse mapping population; 41353149 \- Trudy AIP from DGRP; 32134916 \- Trudy GWAS with DGRP). (not sure if we can say h^2 in flies is like in the range of xx-yy%, I guess numbers from RILs/ILs are higher than selection on longevity due to inbreeding depression).  In *Drosophila melanogaster* longevity is polygenic, fitness adjacent, and measurable in large cohorts under standardized conditions. Candidate gene and pathway work has identified mutations, as well as dietary and drug interventions, that extend fly lifespan. Although work to characterize standing genetic variation that controls lifespan or that interaction with drugs and/or diet has produced ??ambiguous?? results. One explanation for this failure is that longevity is highly polygenic in a manner analogous to human height or BMI, although the scale of experiments carried out to date in Drosophila have likely been insufficient to distinguish polygenicity from a mix of genes of large to intermediate effect against a polygenic background. Here we use extreme QTL (XQTL) mapping in an eight founder advanced intercross synthetic population, phenotyping \>410,000 flies across both sexes and two dietary yeast levels across 10 replicate experiments. Heritable signal is elevated across essentially the entire euchromatic genome in every sex by diet combination. That signal partitions into an average effect plus sex and diet interaction components, and it reorganizes in regionally structured blocks rather than uniformly. One locus rises out of the polygenic background and accounts for 2 to 5% of longevity variation. Natural variation in lifespan does not appear to be concentrated in a set of aging genes (this might need to be revised, or we have to define “aging genes” as a set and show this). It is spread across the genome in a sex and environmental dependent manner.

Linkage based mapping signals act as local integrators of polygenic architecture. In humans, affected sibling pair linkage signals for height and body mass index can be reconstructed quantitatively by summing GWAS effects per variant effects over chromosomal segments (Sidorenko). A multiparent advanced intercross implements that integration directly. Each founder haplotype block carries whatever causal variants happen to segregate within it, and the shift in founder haplotype frequency between control and selected pools measures the aggregate effect of that block. The mapping signal from an extreme mapping experiment is thus a readout of polygenic architecture as a function of genome position. Longevity as a trait is well suited to this experimental approach as the phenotypic tail selects itself, a large cohort is initiated and after some time the small fraction of flies remaining alive are the extreme cohort, with pooled sequencing replacing individual genotyping. Longevity in concert with X-QTL allows us to query hundreds of thousands of flies per sex and diet, and also replicate the experiment at the scale required to detect and quantify subtle linkage signals.

Our implementation follows earlier XQTL experiments in Drosophila \[Macdonald and Long refs\]. The mapping population is the B cage, a synthetic population founded by intercrossing \>600 recombinant inbred lines from the DSPR \[crossing scheme \- I dump 10 eggs from each RIL in a series of vials, wait for adults, then open them in a giant box; this is in my M\&M, but maybe we don’t add anything here?\] and maintained continuously since, with six media bottles added each week and removed after three weeks. All lines descend from eight inbred founder strains with reference quality genome assemblies (King Genetics, Genome Res, Mahul’s paper), and the population has recombined for \[XX\] generations, so founder haplotypes persist only as short blocks. We seeded each aging cage with roughly 10,000 flies of a single sex on a sugar-yeast media containing either 10% (SY10) or 20% yeast (SY20), with SY10 representing a restricted diet that increases lifespan (this could be where we point to the vial experiment I did)? , ~~the dietary axis that sets lifespan in this population~~, held cages at 25°C, replaced food every 2 days, and harvested the last \~500 flies alive after 48-73 days (depending on the sex, diet and replicate). Ten replicates of the X-QTL experiment per sex by diet treatment ran over 18 months. We sequenced pooled DNA from each survivor pool and from a contemporaneous unselected control (collected at the same time as the experimental animals) to 50 to 200X, counted reads at SNPs differentially fixed among the founders, and estimated founder haplotype frequencies in overlapping windows genome wide (Fig. 1a). The contrast between survivor and control pools is the mapping signal. Because the population is an advanced rather than a single generation cross, each 1 cM tile reports the aggregate effect on lifespan of a short haplotype block rather than a whole chromosome arm.

Much of the genome contributes to haplotype change in long lived individuals. Each sex × diet group was scanned independently, contrasting the longest-lived 3–11% of each of 10 replicates per treatment with contemporaneous unselected control individuals (Fig. 1a). Dividing the genetic map into 268 not wholly heterochromatic 1 cM tiles at a \-log10(p) Wald (LWP) threshold of 7.5, 32% of tiles are differentiated (I don’t know what this means practically; there is some kind of statistical test of the actual Wald statistic across the 4 “treatments”?) in at least one treatment and 12% tiles at a threshold of 15\. The mapping population is an advanced- rather than a single-generation cross, and as a result unrecombined founder haplotypes are broken into small blocks and the strongest peaks are correspondingly narrow. We defined eight and ten peaks with local maximum LWP exceeding 15 or 7.5 respectively greater than 5cM apart from one another (Table S1). Constructing 2 LWP support intervals for each of the 18 peaks results in an 80% range on width of 0.25 to 1.51 cM, and of 168 to 828 kb. Wald scores establish that a region shows significant changes in founder haplotype frequencies, but do not estimate the magnitude of each region’s contribution, and small haplotype frequency shifts can be highly significant. The squared changes in founder frequency per window as a function of selected proportions can be used to estimate the heritability explained for each window, which places the scan on a scale of phenotypic variance (Fig. 1b \- given how similar “a” and “b” are, do we need “a” ? I guess its more familiar? Or perhaps Figure 2 \- SNP-based Manhattan plot, replaces “a” ?). LWP and heritability measures are tightly related (r \= 0.98) and heritability can be expressed as a simple function of the number of chromosomes in the sequenced sample and the proportion of individuals in the truncated tail, predicting heritabilities of 0.09%, 0.32% and 0.61% at LWP thresholds of 2, 7.5 and 15 respectively. Despite 0.32% being a subtle heritability estimate of experiment can resolve heritabilities this small and a substantial fraction (is there a \# we can provide?) of the genome is associated with these subtle fractions of variation. This detection limit required screening \~114 thousand flies (This is the average number per sex/diet? If yes, its off, its \>103,000; maybe this impacts the power calculations from later), selecting the longest-lived \~5%, and sequencing several thousand selected and control individuals per treatment. Regions contributing less than 2% to heritable variation would have gone undetected in prior work employing modestly sized mapping panels consisting of several hundred RILs (PMID ​​27485207 is my 805 B RIL paper; could argue the largest QTL in that paper \[explains 5.2%\] overlaps with “3R 8.63” peak from the XQTL), or association type panels consisting of 100s of ILs or 1000s of genotyped individuals (Supplementary Result X). The patterns of variation in heritability we observe throughout the genome is consistent with work attempting to reconcile GWAS hits and affected sib linkage mapping results for human height and BMI (Sidenko), where the authors argue that linkage-based LOD scores are largely consistent with the cumulative effects of underlying polygenes known from large scale GWAS studies.

Perhaps standing genetic variation is depleted because partially recessive alleles are exposed to purifying selection every generation in hemizygous males. On the autosomes 83 of 203 tiles exceed a LWP of 7.5 in at least one of the four treatments. Averaging heritability over the two diets within each sex, male peaks are the highest at 52% of those tiles, so neither sex is systematically more responsive in our experiment. We partitioned the heritability across the four treatments into a main effect, a source due to sex, and a source due to diet (Fig. 1c). Over the tiles with LWP exceeding 7.5, 13.2% of the variation among the four groups is sex-specific and 1.8% diet-specific. It is also apparent from Fig. 1c that the relative partitioning of variation varies as a function of genomic location. (Agreed. But “c” sort of indicates that most of the bigger peaks are main effects, so found in all 4 treatments, right? So is this worth emphasizing? There is this apparent low-level, polygenic signal with main/sex/diset effects, but often when you see a potentially large effect locus, its consistent across diets, and mostly consistent across sexes) This regional variation in genotype by environmental interaction would be refractory to analyses that treat sex and/or environmental variables as covariates removed from phenotypic values before estimating polygenic effects. This would typically be the case in human genetics where the environment is not experimentally manipulated and can vary geographically with genotype. Although longevity in Drosophila under two sugar diets is only a single example, if this observation is general it may have implications for polygenic risk scores.

A large-effect locus sits on top of the polygenic background. The peak on chromosome 3L at 9.30 Mb reaches a LWP of 163.8 in high-sugar males and exceeds 36 in all four groups, in a genome where only 12% of tiles exceed 15 in any group. It accounts for 4.7% of phenotypic variance in high-sugar males and 1.5% in low-sugar females, two to three times the largest of the other regions we detect. It has the narrowest support interval in physical terms of any peak in Table S1 at 55 kb. For this region the change in founder haplotype frequencies is dominated by founder B3 (Fig. 2d), whose frequency decrease in selected pools ranges from 6.3% in low sugar females to 10.3% in high sugar males. This is a much larger allele frequency change than is observed at any other peak. There is no evidence that the haplotype at B3 is unconditionally deleterious as its change in frequency over time in the synthetic population we maintain is typical of other regions and founders (Fig. 2H). B3 represents a naturally occurring allele harboring a factor or factors contributing to poor representation in long lived individuals in both sexes and diets. The mapped interval contains the upstream regulatory region of peptidoglycan recognition protein (PGRP-LA), part of a gene complex that is a component of innate immune signaling in Drosophila, a gene not previously identified as a candidate-gene nor in intervention studies of longevity.

**Outbred multiparental *Drosophila* base population:** Previously we generated a series of Recombinant Inbred Lines (RILs) by taking eight inbred, sequenced founding strains, intercrossing for 50 generations, then producing RILs via 25 generations of inbreeding (22496517, 22505626). The outbred base population used for the present study was created by manually collecting 10 eggs from each of 680 of these population B DSPR (*Drosophila* Synthetic Population Resource) RILs into a series of vials, and releasing the resulting adults into a large 2ft × 2ft × 2ft population cage (BugDorm, 6M610). The base population was initiated in November 2023, and maintained by adding 6 fresh media bottles to the cage every week, simultaneously removing the 6 oldest bottles such that the cage consistently contained 18 bottles. Note that dead animals were never removed, so debris builds up over time in the cage.  
   
**Generating experimental flies for X-QTL mapping:** For each of the 10 X-QTL replicates we collected embryos from the base outbred DSPR B population. Overnight we supplied the cage with a series of apple juice agar plates, each containing a small amount of live yeast paste in the center (Supp Text S1). The following day embryos were removed from the plates, resuspended in PBS, and aliquots of 36-µl were pipeted into a set of media bottles (Supp Text S2). Four days following the emergence of the first adults in these bottles, all flies were transfered to new bottles and allowed to lay eggs overnight. The next day adults were cleared, the media from each bottle was divided into 16 radial sections, and fresh bottles were seeded with a single section. While no egg counting is performed, this process leads to relatively consistent larval densities over bottles.  
   
Two days following the emergence of the first adults, 0-2 day old experimental flies were transferred to fresh bottles. Over the next 2 days flies were sexed/counted via CO2 anesthesia. A small number of males and females were harvested from every source bottle, pooling by sex, to generate groups of "control" flies that represent the base population. Across the 10 replicates, on average we collected single-sex control groups of 694 animals (range \= 610 \- 835). Additionally, we collected groups of 100-150 males and females separately into wide media vials. Vials were kept on their side until 2-4 day old flies were loaded into lifespan cages at the end of the second day of fly collection.  
   
**Lifespan cages, maintenance, and the collection of aged flies:** A series of custom, 22-inch length × 13.75-inch width × 17.5-inch height plexiglass cages were fabricated by the KU Mechanical Prototyping Laboratory (Supp Fig/Text S?). For each of the 10 X-QTL replicates we initiated two lifespan cages per sex, one that received the SY10 diet (10% yeast), and one that received the SY20 diet (20% yeast), splitting all flies collected for that replicate across diet-specific cages. On average, each of the 40 lifespan cages was initiated with 10,399 flies (range \= 8,384 \- 11,281). Each single-sex cohort of experimental flies was maintained in a cage, and provided with 8 new dishes of SY (Sugar-Yeast) media every 48 hours. Any flies dying in the cage, and not being removed on old media remained in the cage. Towards the end of the lifespan of each cohort we endeavored to collect the final 5% of living, aged flies. This was accomplished using an aspirator connected to a vacuum. Given there is no straightforward way to count flies in the lifespan cage environment, there was some variation in the percentage of aged flies we collected; On average we harvested 5.6% of flies (range \= 3.1 \- 10.8%), which averaged 572 flies (range \= 314 \- 1087).  
   
**Fly diets and environments:** All experimental fly rearing, maintenance, and aging was executed in incubators set to 25°C, 60% relative humidity, with a 12 hour : 12 hour light : dark cycle. The parents of the test flies, along with the test flies themselves, were reared and maintained ahead of sexing/counting in 6oz polypropylene stock bottles (Fisher Scientific, Catalog number: AS355) containing 50-ml of cornmeal-yeast-molasses rearing media (Supp Text S3). Following sexing/counting, groups of test flies were maintained in wide, polystyrene vials (Genesee Scientific, Catalog number: 32-117) containing 10-ml of cornmeal-yeast-molasses rearing media (Supp Text S3). Following entry to the lifespan cages, flies were supplied with fresh SY (Sugar-Yeast) media (Supp Text S4) in glass petri dishes every other day. SY media is a commonly-used diet in the *Drosophila* lifespan community, particularly when tests of caloric/dietary restriction are employed (REFS \- MAYBE).  
   
**DNA isolation:** Following collection, single-sex groups of random control and aged flies were maintained in 15-ml tubes at −20°C. DNA isolation employed reagents from the Qiagen/Puregene Cell Kit (Catalog number: 158046), but used a custom protocol enabling isolation of DNA from large amounts of tissue (i.e., 100s of flies; see Supp Text S5). Following isolation, DNA was quantified using the Qubit dsDNA BR Assay Kit (Invitrogen, Catalog Number: Q32850).  
   
**Identifying a lifespan-extending diet for the DSPR B population:** Prior to executing the large-scale X-QTL study we sought to identify appropriate diets to facilitate the experiment. We collected embryos from the outbred base DSPR B population, and used the resulting adults to expand the cohort of flies. In the next generation, vials were cleared of adults, the next day 0-1 day old adults were moved to fresh vials, and the day after that 1-2 day old, very likely mated adults were sexed via CO2 anesthesia and moved to fresh vials in single-sex groups of 20 animals. On the following day, vials of 2-3 day old animals were randomly assigned to 5 dietary treatments (SY2.5, SY5, SY10, SY15, and SY20), differing in the percentage of brewer's yeast (varying from 2.5 to 20%; Supp Text S6). Initially, each sex/treatment combination received 10 vials of 20 flies. Flies were tipped to fresh vials every 2 days, and deaths were recorded daily. Median lifespan, survival curves, and statistical tests comparing curves were executed using the "survival" package (Therneau 2026; version 3.8-6) in R (R Core Team 2025).

Library preparation and sequencing: DNA was prepared on pools of several hundred flies using ?? (Supp table of N of flies \- I have generated this). Illumina DNAseq kit was used for library preparation and was sequenced at UCI Genomics Research and Technology Hub on an Illumina NovaSeq X Plus as 2 × 150 bp reads. Sixty experimental libraries were sequenced: ten replicates of the experiment cages × three groups (unselected control, SY10 selected, SY20 selected) × two sexes. Reads were aligned to the Drosophila melanogaster dm6 reference genome with bwa mem (Li 2013), coordinate sorted and indexed. Experimental sample alignments were not deduplicated although reads from the eight founder alignments were.

SNP calling: SNPs were called on the five major chromosome arms for the eight founder samples and a catalog of SNPs segregating among the eight founders of the synthetic population created. Founders were called jointly with bcftools (cite): a site entered the catalog if it was biallelic, covered at 10× or more in every founder, had a minor allele frequency of 3% or less in every founder, segregating an alternate allele in at least one founder, and was at least 20 bp from the nearest founder indel. The final catalog comprises 1,207,436 SNPs from 1,887,667 initial candidate positions. For each of the 60 experimental samples reference and alternate read counts were then taken directly from the pileup at each catalog position, and these counts used to infer founder haplotype frequencies. At called SNPs autosomal depth averaged 140× per library and a range of 49× to 400×; fifteen libraries fell below 75× and twenty below 100×. In prior work we have shown 50X coverage is sufficient for high quality haplotype estimation.

Haplotype estimation: The synthetic population is derived from eight inbred founders, so a pool’s allele frequency at any SNP is the sum over founders of each founder’s frequency in the pool weighted by its genotype. The founder genotypes are known, so over a local window consisting of many SNPs the eight founder frequencies can be estimated via constrained least squares (lsei, R package limSolve) subject to the frequencies summing to one and each being non-negative. Those frequencies were estimated at 22,420 five kb euchromatic region *steps*, with each step given an initial *window* of ±75 kb, widened in inverse proportion to the local recombination rate so that windows span comparable genetic rather than physical distance. The fit returns a covariance matrix for the estimates which was averaged over the ten steps either side of each step and used in the Wald test (below). Founders genotypes were hierarchically clustered within each window, cut at a height of 2.5, and indistinguishable founders filled by linear interpolation between the means of the flanking resolved steps. The haplotype frequencies were smoothed with a running mean of ±100 kb (41 steps).

**Wald test.** At each step let $\hat{c}$ and $\hat{z}$ be the eight-vectors of estimated founder frequencies in the control and selected pools, and ${V}_{c}$, ${V}_{z}$ their covariance matrices. The Wald-statistic is

$$T=\frac{1}{{R}^{2}} (\hat{c}-\hat{z}{)}^{\top }({V}_{c}+{V}_{z}{)}^{-}(\hat{c}-\hat{z})$$

on seven degrees of freedom, since the eight haplotype frequencies sum to one. That constraint also makes ${V}_{c}+{V}_{z}$ singular, so $(\cdot {)}^{-}$ is a generalised inverse, obtained by eigendecomposition with the null direction discarded and the remaining eigenvalues floored at one per cent of their mean, so that near-degenerate directions cannot inflate $T$. Significance is reported as $-{log}_{10}P$.

Each pool’s covariance is $V=M+\Sigma$, where $M$ is the multinomial sampling covariance on sampled chromosomes with subscript denoting founder alleles,

$${M}_{ff}=\frac{{\overline{p}}_{f}(1-{\overline{p}}_{f})}{{n}_{eff}},  {M}_{fg}=-\frac{{\overline{p}}_{f}{\overline{p}}_{g}}{{n}_{eff}}$$

evaluated at the frequency $\overline{p}$ pooled across the selected and control samples, and $\Sigma$ is the smoothed haplotype reconstruction covariance returned by the constrained least squares fit above. The effective number of individuals is estimated from a pool of $n$ flies (where $k$ is one for male X chromosomes and two otherwise) as

$${n}_{eff}=\frac{kn\sum\limits_{f}^{}{\overline{p}}_{f}(1-{\overline{p}}_{f})}{\sum\limits_{f}^{}{\overline{p}}_{f}(1-{\overline{p}}_{f})+kntr(\Sigma )}$$

The 10 replicates were combined as an ${n}_{eff}$\-weighted mean of $\hat{c}$ and $\hat{z}$, with covariances similarly pooled. As the haplotype frequencies entering $T$ are smoothed, their variance is reduced relative to unsmoothed estimates. ${R}^{2}$, the squared correlation between raw and smoothed frequencies taken over all steps, pools and founders, corrects for this reduction.

**Heritability.** Under truncation selection, retaining the top proportion ${P}_{r}$ of individuals in replicate $r$ corresponds to a standardised selection intensity ${i}_{r}$ (cite Falconer for example). The heritability in the rth replicate, given haplotype frequencies for f founder alleles

$${h}_{r}^{2}=\frac{100 k}{{i}_{r}^{2}}\sum\limits_{f}^{}\frac{\Delta {p}_{fr}^{2}}{{p}_{fr}}$$

with $k$ as defined above and $\Delta {p}_{fr}={\hat{z}}_{fr}-{\hat{c}}_{fr}$.

To obtain an estimate of heritability over all ten replicates we write ${e}_{fr}=\Delta {p}_{fr}/{i}_{r}$ with mean ${\overline{e}}_{f}$ and variance ${s}_{f}^{2}$

$${\hat{h}}^{2}=100 k\sum\limits_{f}^{}\frac{{\overline{e}}_{f}^{ 2}-{s}_{f}^{2}/R}{{\hat{p}}_{f}}$$

where ${\hat{p}}_{f}$ is the mean control frequency and ${s}_{f}^{2}/R$ removes the inflation from squaring an estimate. Being unbiased, ${\hat{h}}^{2}$ can be negative where the true value is near zero.

**The relationship between the Wald test and ${h}^{2}$.** A chi-squared statistic has an expectation equal to its degrees of freedom ($\nu$) plus a non-centrality $\lambda$. In a case-control genome-wide association study $\nu =1$ and $E[{\chi }^{2}]\approx 1+N\cdot 2p(1-p){\beta }^{2}$. Our Wald test has $\nu =7$ degrees of freedom, and $T$ and ${\hat{h}}^{2}$ are likewise both quadratic in the founder frequency shifts, so

$$E[T] \approx  \nu  + \frac{{n}_{eff} {\overline{ı}}^{ 2}}{100 k} {\hat{h}}^{2}$$

where ${n}_{eff}=\sum\limits_{r}^{}{n}_{eff,r}$ and ${\overline{ı}}^{ 2}$ is the ${n}_{eff}$\-weighted mean of ${i}_{r}^{2}$, the second term being the non-centrality $\lambda$. Rearranging gives the line drawn in Supplementary Figure 1\.

The power to detect a region of heritability ${h}^{2}$ at threshold ${T}_{\alpha }$ follows,

$$power = Pr​\left({{\chi }_{\nu }^{2}(\lambda )>{T}_{\alpha }}\right),  \lambda =\frac{NP {i}^{ 2}}{100 k} {h}^{2}$$

for $N$ flies screened per treatment at selected proportion $P$, with $i$ the selection intensity $P$ implies. For example, screening 90,000 flies and selecting the longest-lived 5% ($i=2.06$) gives 80% power at an LWP of 15 (${T}_{\alpha }=85.6$) to detect a region contributing 1% of phenotypic variance. It is apparent from the above equation that halving the target heritability doubles the experiment size in terms of N.

**Partitioning.** We split the ten replicate contrasts in each treatment into two interleaved halves to give eight unbiased estimates of ${\hat{h}}^{2}$ at every step — two sexes $\times$ two diets $\times$ two halves. An orthogonal transformation of those eight numbers gives the heritability shared by all four treatments and the parts specific to sex, to diet, and to their interaction, one degree of freedom each, with the difference between the halves of a treatment carrying four. The five terms are orthogonal, so their sums of squares and degrees of freedom add. We combine the interaction terms with the pure error, as over the significant tiles the median of $M{S}_{sex:diet}/M{S}_{rep}$ is 0.46 against a null median of 0.55, and five of the eighty-five tiles exceed the 5% critical value with four are expected, giving an error variance on five degrees of freedom. Writing $\overline{{\hat{h}}^{2}}$ for the mean of all eight, ${\hat{h}}_{M}^{2}$, ${\hat{h}}_{F}^{2}$, ${\hat{h}}_{SY10}^{2}$, ${\hat{h}}_{SY20}^{2}$ for the marginal means, ${\hat{h}}_{(1)}^{2}$, ${\hat{h}}_{(2)}^{2}$ for the two halves of a treatment and ${d}_{sex:diet}$ for the interaction contrast,

$${d}_{shared}=\overline{{\hat{h}}^{2}},  {d}_{sex}=\frac{1}{2}\left({{\hat{h}}_{M}^{2}-{\hat{h}}_{F}^{2}}\right),  {d}_{diet}=\frac{1}{2}\left({{\hat{h}}_{SY20}^{2}-{\hat{h}}_{SY10}^{2}}\right)$$

$${s}^{2}=\frac{1}{5}\left[{\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{cells}^{}({\hat{h}}_{(1)}^{2}-{\hat{h}}_{(2)}^{2}{)}^{2}+8 {d}_{sex:diet}^{2}}\right]$$

Each component is estimated as $\hat{\sigma }=sign(d)\sqrt{|{d}^{2}-{s}^{2}/8|}$ and tested against the error variance as ${F}_{1,5}=8{d}^{2}/{s}^{2}$, with $Var(d)={s}^{2}/8$ giving the interval $d\pm {t}_{0.975,5}\sqrt{{s}^{2}/8}$.

The partitioning is carried out at every step. To describe genome-wide patterns we also summarize this partitioning and other statistics over 268 non-overlapping one-cM wide tiles spanning the euchromatic genome, with each tile summarised by the step with the largest Wald statistic maximised over the four treatments. The 1cM tile width is chosen to match the mapping resolution of the synthetic population as two-LWP support intervals on peaks (Table S1) have medians of 0.39 cM above an LWP of 15 and 0.76 cM between 7.5 and 15\. Furthermore, 1-cM tiles results in adjacent tiles sharing an ${R}^{2}=81%$ of their variance in the Wald statistic. We summarize statistics over the 85 tiles whose LWP exceeds 7.5, as patterns of variation for non-significant regions are not meaningful.

## Supplementary Result X. The power to detect QTL

A comparison of four experimental paradigms for dissecting complex traits in Drosophila for a locus with heritability ${h}^{2}$ in a base population, phenotypic variance ${V}_{P}=1$ and ${V}_{A}={V}_{E}=0.5$ for automsomes.

**Outbred panel.** $n$ individuals genotyped and phenotyped once, testing a biallelic SNP at a minor allele frequency of 0.15 on one degree of freedom.

**Inbred lines.** $n$ lines, ten measures per line, the same one-degree-of-freedom SNP test applied to line means.

**Eight-way RILs.** $n$ lines, ten measures per line, testing eight founder alleles on seven degrees of freedom.

**X-QTL.** $N$ flies screened, the longest-lived proportion $P$ selected and sequenced in pools against a contemporaneous control, testing eight founder haplotypes on seven degrees of freedom.

Under the alternative test statistics are non-central ${\chi }^{2}$, so

$$power = Pr​\left({{\chi }_{\nu }^{2}(\lambda )>{T}_{\alpha }}\right),  \lambda  = \frac{n {h}^{2}}{1-{h}^{2}}$$

where ${h}^{2}$ is the heritability due to the locus. The line-based designs measure line means rather than individuals, and take ${g}^{2}{\ }$in place of ${h}^{2}$. Inbreeding doubles both the locus variance and the unlinked background and ten measures per line cut the environmental term to ${V}_{E}/10$, giving

$${g}^{2} = \frac{2 {h}^{2}{V}_{P}}{2{V}_{A}+{V}_{E}/10}$$

so for a locus at ${h}^{2}=2%$, ${g}^{2}=3.8%$. For X-QTL the non-centrality is the one given in the Methods. Thresholds are $-{log}_{10}P$ of 6 for the two SNP-based panels reflecting the number of tests carried out, 4 for a RIL linkage scan as established, and 7.5 for X-QTL. For some common designs the power table below (and Supplementary figure 2\) illustrates the limited power of traditional Drosophila approaches for dissecting complex traits.

|  |  | h² |  |  |
| :---- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
|  | n | 2% | 1% | 0.5% |
| Outbred panel | 1,000 | 0.35 | 0.04 | 0.004 |
| Inbred lines | 200 | 0.02 | 0.00 | 0.000 |
| Eight-way RILs | 750 | 0.70 | 0.16 | 0.022 |
| X-QTL | 114,000 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0.894 |

Although X-QTL is the least efficient design "per fly", for traits where bulked phenotyping is an option the overall experiment can be powerful.
